title: Annotatio V §.IV §VII open: five-proof vindication last; Oral among testamentary goods?
pass_a_gloss: §. VII. But indeed the vindication of these proofs, reduced to the number five, is the last of all those things by which it was pleasant to him to come forth into disputatory battle against me, Christianly seeking peace and union with his Church — whose weakness after we have shown, we will set an end to our Annotation on the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body, and to the Disputation against its Truth in part, and in part, if Truth be supposed, against its Fundamentalitatem, or Necessity to salvation either for believing or for doing. But as the most Famous Professor’s first Proof — that the Article on the Sacred Supper is fundamental, or more rightly, that the Oral Eating of Christ’s Body in the Sacred Supper cannot, faith being safe (as the Author’s words have it), be rashly wounded by anyone, or weakened, much less denied — has its strength placed in this, that it supposes Oral Eating to be numbered among the goods bequeathed to us by our Savior in the testament, so that, when the Author had noticed that the Oral Eating so greatly commended by him is in no way counted by me among our Savior’s Testamentary goods properly so called, as pertaining to Christ’s disciples alone, His true and only heirs and co-heirs, he contends that Testamentary Goods which deserve to be so called are to be judged not from the heirs’ condition but from the things’ own nature and the Testator’s will: And that distinction is also to be made between Testamentary Goods and the Commodities overflowing from those goods, §. XV.
pass_b_english: §.VII: last of five proofs — then this Oral Annotation ends. The first proof’s strength is counting Oral among testamentary goods bequeathed by the Savior.

Because Strimesius will not count Oral among testamentary goods proper to Christ’s true heirs alone, the Author (§.XV) says judge such goods by the testator’s will/nature of the things, and distinguish goods from overflowing commodities.
source_text: §. VII. Verùm enim verò probationum harum, ad quinarium numerum redactarum vindicatio, postremum eorum omnium est, quô in aciem disputatoriam adversus me, pacem unionémque cum ejus Ecclesiâ Christianè ambientem, prodire ipsi volupe fuit, cujus imbecillitatem postquam ostenderimus, Annotationi nostræ de Manducatione Corporis Christi Orali, Disputationíque contra istius partim Veritatem, partim, si Veritas supponatur, Fundamentalitatem, seu ad salutem vel creditu, vel factu, Necessitatem, finem imponemus. Sicuti verò prima Clarissimi Professoris Probatio, Articulum de S. Cœna fundamentalem esse, vel rectiùs, Oralem Corporis Christi in S. Cœna Manducationem, salvâ, (ut habent verba Autoris) hominis fide, lædi à quoquam temerè, aut infirmari, nedum negari, posse, in eo robur suum collocatum habet, quòd Oralis Manducatio inter bona à Servatore nostro, testamento nobis legata, annumeranda supponit, ita, ut, cùm advertisset Autor, tantopere à se commendatam Oralem Manducationem, Testamentariis Salvatoris nostri bonis propriè dictis, à me neutiquam accenseri, ceu ad solos Christi discipulos, veros unicosque hæredes ejus & cohæredes, pertinentibus, contendit, Bona Testamentaria quæ merentur dici, non ex conditione hæredum, sed ex ipsâ rerum natura & voluntate Testatoris, esse judicandum: Distinguendum item esse inter Bona Testamentaria & inter Commoda ex bonis istis redundantia, §. XV.
notes: §VII: five proofs; Oral as testamentary good?
